b: Replicants in the Blade Runner universe are bioengineered humanoids that look and sound like real people but lack a capacity for human emotion. It’s an apt metaphor for the slew of recent TV shows—including HBO’s leaden Dune: Prophecy and Hulu’s fatuous Alien: Earth—that attempt to replicate the magic of sci-fi IP on the small screen.

Set 80 years after the events of Ridley Scott’s landmark sci-fi noir Blade Runner, Blade Runner 2099 initially seems like another shareholder-minded exercise in rehabilitating a franchise that probably should have been retired long ago. The difference is that Amazon’s series grounds its impeccable world-building in a story that’s both gripping and affecting, ultimately affording it the ineffable quality any corporate-born abomination craves: a soul.

Unlike so many franchise TV spinoffs constrained by the whims of their predecessors’ plots, Blade Runner 2099 quickly establishes itself as an evolution of the franchise’s tenets. An opening crawl explains that in the five decades since Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049, the Nexus-9 replicant models overthrew their creators, establishing a new world order in which replicants oversee the human underclass. To keep them in check, the police enlist a special squadron of “blade runners” to hunt down anyone who once rebelled against the humanoids.

This spells trouble for Cora (Hunter Schafer), a scrappy drifter whose single-minded focus on securing visas for herself and her dispossessed brother (Lewis Gribben) sees her secretly taking on the identity of a ruthless blade runner. She’s partnered with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a blade runner nearing the end of her predetermined lifespan and searching for a runaway replicant who may hold the key to both Cora’s salvation and Olwen’s survival.

Centering the narrative on this flipped power dynamic opens the series up to slipperier questions about the nature of man versus machine in our own technologically precarious world. And while most other dystopian series would focus on the action of the revolution itself, the Blade Runner franchise has always been more attuned to the ways in which geopolitics and humanity’s Freudian death drive play out at the individual level: on rain-splattered sidewalks and cluttered apartments rather than situation rooms and battlefields.

Visually capturing that level of detail, Blade Runner 2099 flourishes. From splashes of neon piercing through window shades to the soot and rust eating away at the ramshackle equipment, this is fine-tuned cyberpunk production design. There’s a startling glamour to the show’s most meditative images—smokestacks sinking into oceans of sand before a boiling sun, 400-story skyscrapers disappearing into L.A.’s smog—which are not only expertly realized but, alongside Leopold Ross’s sweeping electro-jazz score, conjure an atmosphere of punishing decay.

While the plot of Blade Runner 2099 can sometimes get needlessly convoluted and the precise existential stakes difficult to parse, creator Silka Luisa has a knack for bringing audiences back to the show’s most bare-bones elements, namely an engaging mystery and a pair of protagonists worth following to the end. Schafer plays Cora with a rousing, coiled physicality, while Yeoh’s leonine features and disciplined vocal modulation lend her character an icy ferocity that makes her glimmers of remorse and wonderment all the more affecting.

The casting of Schafer and Yeoh, and the way Cora’s and Olwen’s objectives gradually intertwine, brings to mind “A Cyborg Manifesto,” Donna Haraway’s seminal essay that uses the notion of the human-machine hybrid to advocate for a socialist feminism built on coalition through shared values rather than identity politics. Blade Runner 2099’s ethos may not be as radical as that text, but the show’s subtle portrait of how capitalism-induced loneliness erodes one’s propensity for human connection proves especially poignant. A sequence at a seedy club where replicants indulge their desire for reproduction by donning pregnancy prosthetics is one of many that demonstrate how the series isn’t content merely to replicate its originator’s philosophical threads, but elaborates on them.

Still, there’s something spine-tingling about the fact that this series, about how corporate greed and heedless bioengineering lead to humanity’s subjugation and the planet’s deterioration, comes from the same company whose data centers are helping destroy the rainforest it’s named after. As entertainment, Blade Runner 2099 is a wild success, but on a meta level, its disturbing dystopia might not even be as disturbing as our reality.
